content: The case series by Leochico and Valera (2020) was evaluated based on specific criteria to assess its methodological rigor and reliability. Below are the detailed findings: 1. The inclusion criteria for participants in the case series were not clearly defined, making it unclear whether the selection process was systematic or arbitrary. 2. The condition under investigation was not measured in a standardized or reliable manner across all participants, and this aspect was deemed not applicable (NA). 3. Similarly, the methods used to identify the condition in participants were not applicable (NA), raising concerns about the consistency of diagnostic approaches. 4. The study ensured consecutive inclusion of participants, which strengthens the representativeness of the sample and reduces selection bias. 5. However, the case series did not achieve complete inclusion of all eligible participants, which may introduce bias or limit the generalizability of the findings. 6. The demographics of the participants were clearly reported, providing essential context for understanding the study population. 7. Clinical information about the participants was also clearly reported, ensuring transparency and aiding in the interpretation of the findings. 8. The outcomes or follow-up results of the cases were clearly reported, allowing for an accurate assessment of the intervention's impact or the condition's progression. 9. The demographic information of the presenting sites or clinics was clearly reported, which adds to the contextual understanding of the study. 10. Statistical analysis was deemed appropriate for the study, ensuring that the data were analyzed in a manner consistent with the research objectives. The overall score for this case series was 6 out of a possible 8 (excluding NA items), which places it in the moderate quality category. This indicates that while the study has several strengths, such as clear reporting of demographics and clinical information, there are notable limitations, particularly in the areas of inclusion criteria and standardization of condition measurement. For mixed-methods studies, the evaluation of Di Marco et al. (2003) highlighted the following: 1. The research questions were clearly stated, ensuring that the study's objectives were well-defined. 2. The data collected were sufficient to address the research questions, demonstrating that the study design was aligned with its goals. 3. The qualitative approach used was appropriate for answering the research questions, ensuring methodological congruence. 4. The methods for qualitative data collection were adequate, supporting the validity of the findings. 5. The findings were derived appropriately from the data, ensuring that the conclusions were grounded in evidence. 6. The interpretation of results was sufficiently substantiated by the data, providing a robust basis for the study's conclusions. 7. There was coherence between the qualitative data sources, collection methods, analysis, and interpretation, ensuring consistency throughout the study. For randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the study by Hansen, Tresse, and Gunnarsson (2004) was critically appraised: 1. True randomization was used for assigning participants to treatment groups, ensuring that allocation bias was minimized. 2. Allocation to treatment groups was concealed, further reducing the risk of selection bias. 3. The treatment groups were similar at baseline, ensuring comparability and reducing confounding variables. 4. Participants were not blinded to treatment assignment, but this was deemed not applicable (NA) for the study design. 5. Those delivering the treatment were also not blinded, which was similarly marked as not applicable (NA). 6. Outcome assessors were not clearly blinded to treatment assignment, making it unclear (UC) whether this potential source of bias was addressed. 7. Treatment groups were treated identically, except for the intervention of interest, ensuring that differences in outcomes could be attributed to the intervention. 8. Follow-up was complete, and any differences between groups in terms of follow-up were adequately described and analyzed. 9. Participants were analyzed in the groups to which they were randomized, ensuring adherence to the intention-to-treat principle. 10. Outcomes were measured in the same way for all treatment groups, ensuring consistency in data collection. 11. Outcomes were measured reliably, supporting the validity of the findings. 12. Appropriate statistical analysis was used, ensuring that the results were interpreted correctly. 13. The trial design was appropriate, and any deviations from the standard RCT design were accounted for in the conduct and analysis of the trial. The RCT received a score of 10 out of 11, placing it in the high quality category. This indicates that the study was methodologically robust, with minimal risk of bias and strong internal validity. For quasi-experimental studies, the study by Hoenig et al. (2005) was evaluated: 1. There was no ambiguity regarding the temporal relationship between variables, ensuring clarity in causal inference. 2. Participants included in comparisons were similar, reducing the risk of confounding. 3. Participants in comparisons received similar treatment or care, except for the intervention of interest, ensuring that differences in outcomes could be attributed to the intervention. 4. A control group was included, strengthening the study's ability to draw causal inferences. 5. Multiple measurements of the outcome were conducted both before and after the intervention, enhancing the reliability of the findings. 6. Follow-up was complete, and any differences between groups in terms of follow-up were adequately described and analyzed. 7. Outcomes for participants in comparisons were measured in the same way, ensuring consistency in data collection. 8. Outcomes were measured reliably, although this aspect was marked as unclear (UC). 9. Appropriate statistical analysis was used, ensuring that the results were interpreted correctly. The quasi-experimental study received a score of 8 out of 9, placing it in the high quality category. This indicates that the study was well-conducted, with strong methodological rigor and reliable findings. These detailed evaluations provide a comprehensive understanding of the methodological strengths and limitations of the studies reviewed, ensuring that their findings can be interpreted with appropriate caution and confidence.
